name: Fulfulde of the Foulbé du Baguirmi, 'dialecte foul parlé par les Foulbé du Baguirmi'
confidence_why: The only description of this variety, Gaden 1908, places the accent on the root in the intensive future and in the negative present/future but on the suffix vowel in the negative aorist, so stress marks grammatical form; the one differing placement, the suffix-stressed negative -ataa of Pelletier & Skinner 1979, belongs to Adamawa Fulfulde of Nigeria, another dialect.
catalog_citation: Gaden, Henri. 1908. Note sur le dialecte foul parlé par les Foulbé du Baguirmi. Journal Asiatique, 10e série, tome 11 (janvier-février 1908): 5-70. [Printed header reads 'Note'; Glottolog ref 76114 has 'Notes'. Scan: archive.org dli.ministry.15314; second scan;ernet.dli.2015.530756.]
catalog_locator: Journal pp. 22 (Futur, 2°, the -oto intensive future), 25 (De quelques contractions), 26 (De la voix négative: Aoriste) and 27 (Présent et futur)27, 28, 29, root structure: 'Des racines', journal pp. 9-10. Phonology section 'Matériel phonétique' pp. 8-9 has no accent statement.
catalog_quote: [p. 22, Futur 2°, after the examples gorko 'on dod'oto « cet homme va certainement tomber »; pul'a ma sikdoto « ton cheval boitera certainement »; d'emma fu gaba wurtoto « toutes les nuits l'hippopotame sort »:] L'accent tonique porte sur la racine et est très marqué. [p. 26, De la voix négative, Aoriste:] La négation s'exprime par la suffixation de a'i; ainsi: mi wara'i « je ne suis pas venu »; mo tat'a'i « il n'a pas coupé ». ... Dans les deux cas d'aoriste négatif en a'i et aki l'accent porte sur l'a du suffixe. [p. 27, Présent et futur, negative in -ata / -a:] mi warata « je ne viendrai pas »; mi danata « je ne dormirai pas ». ... Quelques verbes forment un présent négatif en suffixant simplement a: yidgo « aimer »; mi yidi « j'aime »; mi yida « je n'aime pas »; mi yidat « j'aimerai »; mi yidata « je n'aimerai pas ». Dans tous ces cas, à la voix négative, la voyelle radicale est nettement accentuée. [p. 25, De quelques contractions] a hokatayam de ? « tu me la donneras? » [En accentuant spécialement la voyelle radicale on donnerait le sens négatif: « tu ne me la donneras pas? ».]

new_statements.translation: [p. 22:] The tonic accent falls on the root and is very marked. [p. 26:] In both cases of the negative aorist in -a'i and -aki the accent falls on the a of the suffix. [p. 27:] In all these cases, in the negative voice, the root vowel is clearly accented. [p. 25:] a hokatayam de? 'will you give it to me?' [By specially accenting the root vowel one would give the negative sense 'won't you give it to me?'.]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Gaden gives no general phonological rule. His remarks, all inside the verb morphology, say the accent normally sits on the root (the root vowel = first syllable of a Fula word) and is strongly marked, including in the negative present/future in -ata/-a; the one stated exception is the negative aorist in -a'i/-aki, where the accent moves to the suffix vowel a. He also notes that accent placement can distinguish an affirmative future (a hokat-a-yam) from its negative (a hokata-yam) when the segmental forms coincide. The p. 22 sentence is placed in the paragraph on the -oto intensive future and may be meant only for that form; the p. 27 sentence generalizes root accent to all negative present/future forms. Nearest-dialect grammars (Taylor 1921, Adamawa) describe the same facts as vowel-length-driven stress with final accent in the negative past, so a weight-sensitive analysis is plausible but is not what Gaden says.
new_statements.exceptions: Negative aorist in -a'i / -aki: accent on the suffix a (p. 26). Accent on the root vowel as a mark of negation when the affirmative and negative verb forms would otherwise sound alike (p. 25).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remarks on finite verb forms only (affirmative vs. negative tenses); nothing on nouns, phrases or citation forms. Gaden states (p. 8) that he is not writing a grammar but noting differences from Senegambian Fula (de Guiraudon's Manuel and notation), so the accent remarks are incidental, not a phonology statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Gaden 1908 describes the Fulfulde of the Foulbé of Baguirmi (Chad), i.e. bagi1244 itself, from material collected during a stay of nearly three years (c. 1903-1906); he traces these Fulbe to the Diamaré (Adamawa) and treats the dialect as closest to Adamawa Fulfulde (fub, adam1253), contrasting it throughout with Senegambian Fula (de Guiraudon). The Wikipedia-listed Harrison 2003 report is a family-level survey. Taylor 1921 (also saved) is Adamawa Fulfulde, kept only as nearest-dialect context.

readall_conflicts: No new source about Bagirmi Fulfulde itself was opened, so the catalog record (Gaden 1908, form-specific remarks, 'morphologically determined') stands unchanged. The one cross-dialect tension: Pelletier & Skinner (Adamawa Fulfulde, Nigeria) put the stress on the first a of the negative suffix -ataa, whereas Gaden (Bagirmi) says that in the negative present/future in -ata the radical vowel is clearly accented (p. 27), while placing the accent on the suffix a in the negative aorist -a'i/-aki (p. 26). Since the two works describe different varieties, this is a dialect difference or a difference in description, not a contradiction within the bagi1244 record.

sources.citation: Taylor, F. W. 1921. A first grammar of the Adamawa dialect of the Fulani language (Fulfulde). Oxford: Clarendon Press. [NEAREST-DIALECT CONTEXT ONLY — Adamawa Fulfulde, not Bagirmi]
sources.note: §7 'Accent' (p. 18): 'The accent is predominantly a stress accent, and, generally speaking, depends on the long vowels' — long first/penultimate vowel takes the accent, otherwise first syllable; final-syllable accent in the negative past ('o warai, he did not come'). Consistent with Gaden's suffix-accented negative aorist -a'i, but this is Adamawa (fub), not Bagirmi.

No mention of stress, accent or tone; only a generic consonant/vowel sentence. Cites Gaden 1908 and Harrison 2003 (SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2003-009, 'Fulfulde language family report', 13 pp.), the 2009 Chad alphabet decree and Priest & Hosken 2010 (Unicode).

sources.note: Gaden (pp. 6-7) says the Baguirmi Fulbe came from the Diamaré/Adamawa and have their closest linguistic affinities with Adamawa Fulfulde; a modern reference grammar of that dialect is the best proxy for a systematic stress rule, and Taylor 1921 already frames Adamawa stress as vowel-length driven. Not Bagirmi-specific, so it cannot replace Gaden for the catalog, only contextualize him.
